Judgment
Amal Ranaraja. J,
1. The accused-appellant (hereinafter referred to as the “appellant”) has
been indicted in the High Court of Hambantota in Case
No.HC/54/2020. The charges in the indictment are as follows;
01. On or around the 04th of July 2015, within the jurisdiction of
this Court, in Suriyawewa, you, have committed rape against
one Loku Wahumpurage Jeewanthi Kumarathunga, a minor,
under the age of 16; hence, committed an offence punishable
under Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka as
amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995.
02. On or around the 04th of July 2015, within the jurisdiction of
this Court, in Suriyawewa, you, in order to gain some sexual
gratification have used a certain part of your body, on one
Loku Wahumpurage Jeewanthi Kumarathunga, a person
under 16 years of age, i.e. by placing your male genitalia near
her female genitalia; hence, committed “Grave Sexual Abuse”,
an offence punishable under Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal
Code of Sri Lanka as amended by Penal Code (Amendment)
Act No.22 of 1995 and No. 29 of 1998.
2. At the conclusion of the trial, the appellant has been convicted of the
first and acquitted of the second charge and sentenced as follows;
i. 11 years rigorous imprisonment and fined a sum of Rs.
10,000.00 with a term of 6 months rigorous imprisonment in
default.
The appellant has also been directed to pay a sum of
Rs.400,000.00 as compensation to PW01 with a term of 1 year
simple imprisonment in default.
Case of the Prosecution
3. On the day of the incident, PW01 and her grandmother have decided to
go to PW01’s uncle’s place to spend the night. While on their way, PW01
has realised that she had forgotten the clothes that were necessary to
attend Sunday school the next day. PW01 has then returned home to
fetch these clothes. At that time, the appellant has entered the house
and had penile-vaginal intercourse with PW01 against her will.
Case of the Appellant
4. The appellant has contended that he went to the residence of PW01 at
her invitation. He has denied having penile-vaginal intercourse with
PW01 in that instance.
Grounds of Appeal
5. When the matter was taken up for argument, the learned counsel
appearing on behalf of the appellant, urged the following grounds of
appeal.
I. Has the learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the
evidence of the prosecutrix had not been corroborated by
independent evidence, and analyse as to whether it was safe to
convict the accused on her sole testimony?
II. Could the conviction be sustained due to the failure of the learned
High Court Judge to neither reject nor accept the dock statement
and thereby conclude that the dock statement has not caused a
reasonable doubt in the prosecution case?
III. Did the learned High Court Judge misdirect himself by arriving
at the conclusion that the prosecutrix, who was 12 years of age
at the time of the incident, will not engage in an act of self-
satisfaction in the absence of any evidence or without having the
opportunity to observe the demeanour of the prosecutrix whilst
giving evidence?
IV. Has the learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the
prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt?
V. Did the learned High Court Judge misdirect himself by failing to
consider that the prosecution did not place before Court, the
evidence of PW03 and PW04, to whom the prosecutrix is alleged
to have divulged the incident and whether the said failure caused
reasonable doubt in the prosecution case?
6. The case under consideration involves a young girl (PW01), who was
merely 12 years old at the time of the incident and had provided
testimony six years later. The complexities of recalling events from a
young age pose challenges, including potential for inconsistencies and
exaggeration.
7. To begin with, it is crucial to acknowledge the psychological aspects of
memory. Children possess cognitive faculties that are still developing.
Children experience difficulties in accurately recalling events, especially
those that are traumatic or extraordinary. As years pass the details may
become increasingly blurred, influenced by various factors, such as
discussions with peers, media exposure, or even parental input. The
likelihood of inconsistencies creeping into the testimony becomes
significant as memories are not fixed but rather, can evolve over time.
Hence, it is reasonable to expect a child’s account of an event to contain
inaccuracies, particularly several years later.
8. It is essential to consider the context in which these narratives are
made. The child may not remember specific details or may exaggerate
his/her narrative but may still convey the core truth of an incident.
Courts must evaluate whether the inconsistencies affect the substance
of the testimony, or if they pertain to peripheral details that do not alter
the fundamental truth of what has transpired.
9. Furthermore, placing undue emphasis on minor inconsistencies risks
undermining the very essence of justice. It is vital for the judicial system
to remain accessible and fair to vulnerable populations, such as
children. If Courts were to dismiss the entire testimony of a child
witness based on minor inconsistencies, it could deter future witnesses
from coming forward.
10. While alleged inconsistencies and exaggeration in the testimony of
PW01 warrant careful consideration, they should not automatically
invalidate her account. Especially, when such discrepancies are not
material to the core of her account.
11. The discrepancies in PW01’s testimony relate to several points. They
are, the location in the house where the appellant accosted PW01, the
reported duration of the incident, the specific room in which the
incident occurred, and the manner in which PW01 resisted prior to the
incident.
12. This Court deems such discrepancies not to be fundamental to PW01’s
testimony and consequently not material. Moreover, PW01 has
maintained consistency regarding the core incident involving the
appellant, specifically the penile-vaginal intercourse committed on
PW01.
13. In the case of R v B [2010] EWCA Crim 4 The Lord Chief Justice of
England and Wales, has held as follows;
“We emphasise that in our collective experience the age of a witness is
not determinative on his or her ability to give truthful and accurate
evidence. Like adults some children will provide truthful and accurate
testimony, and some will not. However, children are not miniature
adults, but children, and to be treated and judged for what they are, not
what they will, in years ahead, grow to be. Therefore, although due
allowance must be made in the trial process for the fact that they are
children with, for example, a shorter attention span than most adults,
none of the characteristics of childhood, and none of the special
measures which apply to the evidence of children carry with them the
implicit stigma that children should be deemed in advance to be
somehow less reliable than adults. The purpose of the trial process is to
identify the evidence which is reliable and that which is not, whether it
comes from an adult or a child.”
14. Further, in the case of AG v. Daradadagamage Chandraratne,
CA/85/2013, decided on 25.05.2018, S. Thurairaja PC, J, has held as
follows,
“Time and again Courts have discussed the acceptance of evidence of
children of tender ages. Our Judges are not there to test the memory of
the witness, they are expected to Eind the actual fact and the truth.
Witnesses are human being, they are not memory machines nor robots
to repeat the incident as it was. Further the natural behaviour of
human beings is to forget incidents, especially sad memories. No one
wants to re- visit painful moments and keep detailed memories with
them. We are also mindful most of our courts, with due respect, are not
child friendly. In this case a child giving evidence after 8 years and
subjected to cross examination more than 3 years is sufEicient to create
certain contradictions in her testimony. It is human nature.”
15. The Superior Courts in Sri Lanka have held that inter-labial
penetration, meaning contact with, or slight entry between the labia,
without full internal insertion, or the rapture of the hymen, is sufficient
to satisfy the penetration required for the offence of rape. Complete
insertion or tearing of the hymen is not required to prove that
penetration occurred
16. In the case of Perera Vs. The Attorney General (2012) 1 SLR 69, Ranjith
Silva J, has held as follows,
“In the book entitled The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and
Toxicology, Dr. K.S. Narayana Reddy at page 308 states as follows:
“The slightest penetration of the penis within the vulva, such as the
minimal passage of glands between the labia or with or without the
emission of semen or rupture of hymen constitutes rape. There need
not be a completed act of intercourse. Rape can be committed even
when there is inability to produce a penile erection. Rape can occur
without causing any injury and as such negative evidence does not
exclude rape.”
It is my view that one should analyse the evidence in this case in the
light of the above-mentioned expert medical opinion as the opinion
expressed above is the opinion of almost all the text writers on forensic
medicine and it has gained such notorious that any quote can take
judicial notice of the same.”
17. PW01, prior to being examined by Dr. A.S. Senevirathne, Consultant
Judicial Medical Officer has, in her history, stated as follows
Vide Page 272 of the Case Brief
i.e. That the appellant placed his penis on her vagina and made up and
down movements thereafter, indicating that the appellant had
penetrated her. Upon examining PW01, Dr. Senevirathne has prepared
a medico-legal report. This report has been produced as evidence
marked පැ 01. Following the examination, Dr. Senevirathne has opined
as follows;
“There were features suggestive of intercourse possibly inter labial”
Vide Page 274 of the Case Brief
18. The statement of PW01 to Dr. Senevirathne, as referred to above
indicates that she has remained consistent with respect to the core
incident involving the appellant. Furthermore, Dr. Senevirathne’s
opinion corroborates the same.
19. Further, the learned High Court Judge in pages 13 and 14 of his
judgement has stated as follows;
Vide Pages 158-159 of the Case Brief
i.e. That the evidence presented by the appellant fails to raise a
reasonable doubt regarding the prosecution’s case. As a result, the
learned High Court Judge has in effect, discredited the appellant’s
narrative and disregarded the same. Therefore, the argument asserting
that the learned High Court Judge has not rejected the appellant’s
evidence cannot be upheld.
20. In the domain of law, the concept of probability plays a crucial role in
determining the outcome of trials. The test of probability assesses how
likely an event is to occur or a claim to be true, based on available
evidence.
21. In the case of Wickramasuriya v Dedoleena and Others [1996] 2 SLR 95,
F.N.D. Jayasuriya J, has held,
“A Judge, in applying the Test of Probability and Improbability relies
heavily on his knowledge of men and matters and the patterns of
conduct observed by human beings both ingenious as well as those who
are less talented and fortunate.
If the contradiction is not of that character the Court ought to accept
the evidence of witnesses whose Evidence is otherwise cogent having
regard to the Test of Probability and Improbability and having regard
to his demeanour and deportment manifested by witnesses. Trivial
contradictions which do not touch the core of a party's case should not
be given much signiEicance, specially when the probabilities factor
echoes in favour of the version narrated by an applicant.”
22. PW01 has testified that when she was initially accosted by the
appellant, she screamed for help however, the appellant has then
gagged her with his fist, which has prevented her from continuing to
scream.
Given these circumstances, it is probable that PW01 would not have
been screaming at the moment PW02, Wewala Gamage Nuwan Lakmal,
an uncle of PW01, arrived at the scene of the incident.

23. The appellant has also contended although PW01 had an opportunity
to divulge the incident involving the appellant to PW02 at the initial
instance, i.e. when PW02 arrived at the location the incident occurred,
that she has not done so. Consequently, PW01 has not been
spontaneous in disclosing the incident.
24. It appears that PW02, who is PW01’s uncle, had slapped PW01
immediately after confronting her about the incident involving the
appellant. After slapping PW01, PW02 has directed her to go to the
house, in which her grandmother was at that time, immediately. All this
has happened very quickly and PW01 has had no opportunity to explain
the situation to PW02.
25. Given these circumstances, it is understandable why PW01 did not
disclose the incident involving the appellant to PW02 at that moment.
However, PW01 upon arriving at the house in which her grandmother
was in, has divulged the incident involving the appellant to her relatives
present therein.
26. Consequent to such disclosure, a police complaint has been lodged the
very next day. In those circumstances, the contention that PW01 has
not been spontaneous in disclosing the incident involving the appellant
must fail.
27. Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance No. 14 of 1895 reads as
follows:
“No particular number of witnesses shall in any case be required for the proof of any fact.” 28. The primary implication of Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance is
the adoption of the principle that “evidence must not be counted but
weighed”. This has several key consequences in the Sri Lankan legal
system. A court can convict an accused or determine a case solely on
the uncorroborated evidence of a single witness provided that the judge
finds that witness to be cogent, credible, trustworthy and impressive.
29. The law does not require corroboration of witness’s testimony as an
essential condition for a conviction. The trial Judge has the discretion
to rely on the testimony if satisfied with its veracity after careful
probing. The emphasis is shifted from a mere head count of witnesses
to a careful judicial analysis and evaluation of the witness’s demeanour,
consistency, and overall trustworthiness of his testimony.
30. In Sumanasena v Attorney General [1999] 3 SLR 137, Jayasuriya J.
has held as follows:
“Evidence must not be counted but weighed and the evidence of a single
solitary witness if cogent and impressive could be acted upon by a Court
of law.”
31. Consequently, the learned High Court Judge was correct in considering
the testimony of PW01 and acting upon it.
32. It appears that the first formal complaint about the incident involving
the appellant has been lodged with the investigators on the very next
day, as PW09 (Officer in Charge of the Suriyawewa Police Station,
Inspector of Police Jayasinghe) has stated. This timing supports PW01’s
narrative that she reported the incident to her grandmother and an
aunt at the earliest opportunity.
33. Given this sequence of events the prosecution’s decision not to call
PW03 and PW04 could be readily understood, as their testimony would
have been cumulative, merely repeating facts already confirmed by
PW01’s prompt disclosure and the subsequent complaint.
34. Due to the matters discussed above, I am not inclined to interfere with
the conviction, judgement and the sentencing order imposed on the
appellant and proceed to affirm the same.
35. I dismiss the appeal but make no order regarding costs.
Appeal dismissed.
36. The term of rigorous imprisonment shall commence from the date this
judgement is conveyed to the appellant in the High Court of
Hambantota.
37. The Registrar of this Court is directed to send this Judgement to the
High Court of Hambantota for compliance.
